abstract: |
  Supplemental Poverty Measure (SPM) thresholds reflect spending on basic
  needs as well as prices. BLS re-estimates them from a rolling five-year
  Consumer Expenditure Survey window and publishes them in the following
  year. Poverty projections therefore require an estimate of thresholds
  that simple inflation adjustment need not reproduce. This paper sets
  out the threshold calculation, implements an approximate replication
  from public microdata, and compares price-based and consumption-based
  projection rules. Under the current research method, retrospective
  2020–2025 mean absolute errors across housing tenures average 2.29 percent
  for CPI-U adjustment, 1.65 percent for a composite price index, 0.51
  percent for replicated consumption growth, and 0.90 percent for an
  equal blend of the latter two. These comparisons use revised data and
  overlapping estimation windows. A distinct, pre-committed 2025 nowcast
  supplies one external validation year: the blend's mean absolute error
  was 1.17 percent against 2.58 percent for CPI-U adjustment and 0.75
  percent for consumption growth alone. The largest miss was for renters.
  For years beyond available microdata, a separate conditional projection
  advances both expenditure and rent windows through 2035, with explicit
  assumptions about prices and real spending. Its prospective accuracy
  has not been established.
  Sample-treatment sensitivities and unreplicated imputations limit
  claims about level accuracy and future performance. The results support
  evaluating consumption growth when projecting quasi-relative poverty
  thresholds, while keeping retrospective comparisons separate from
  forecasts made before publication.
---

# Introduction

The Supplemental Poverty Measure (SPM) defines a poverty threshold that
changes with expenditure patterns as well as prices. Its national
thresholds come from Consumer Expenditure (CE) Interview Survey spending
on food, clothing, shelter, utilities, telephone, and internet; they vary
by housing tenure and are adjusted for family composition and local
housing costs [@itwg2010; @garner2021]. This quasi-relative design follows
the National Academy of Sciences proposal to update basic-needs standards
with consumption over time [@citro1995].

The publication calendar creates a practical estimation problem. BLS
publishes thresholds in the following year: the 2024 thresholds appeared
in September 2025, and the 2025 thresholds on August 24, 2026
[@p60-287; @bls2025thresholds]. An analysis conducted before publication
must estimate the threshold as well as SPM resources. Adjusting the
last published threshold for inflation accounts for price changes, but
not necessarily changes in the expenditure distribution from which BLS
re-estimates the threshold.

Existing poverty projections illustrate several responses to this gap.
Urban Institute projections for 2021 adjusted the 2019 thresholds for
projected inflation [@wheaton2021]. Columbia's monthly poverty framework
initially carried the latest published thresholds forward, identifying
the need for more timely consumption data to project new ones
[@parolin2022]. Price adjustment also has a separate
measurement purpose: anchored-SPM series hold a reference standard fixed
in real terms to distinguish changes in resources and policy from changes
in living standards [@wimer2016; @nasem2019]. That estimand differs from
predicting the thresholds BLS will publish.

This paper examines the latter task. It first describes national threshold
estimation and its application to SPM units. It then reconstructs
thresholds from public CE files, quantifies selected methodological
sensitivities, and compares four one-year projection rules. The main
research experiment uses the current implementation for 2019–2025
replication and 2020–2025 retrospective projections. A separately frozen
2020–2024 comparison and pre-committed 2025 nowcast document the method
used before the 2025 outcome was published. The completed 2025 evaluation
provides one external validation year; the current retrospective results
do not add further prospective observations.

The final methodological extension addresses years beyond available
microdata. It advances the CE and American Community Survey (ACS) windows
under declared price, real-expenditure, and rent assumptions. This
distinguishes an observed expenditure nowcast from a conditional forecast
whose future survey records must themselves be projected.

# Calculating the thresholds {#sec-production}

## National reference thresholds

BLS estimates a national threshold for a two-adult, two-child reference
unit in each of three housing tenures: owners with a mortgage, owners
without a mortgage, and renters. Census applies the thresholds to SPM
resource units after adjusting for composition and local housing costs,
and computes poverty status from the corresponding resources
[@itwg2010; @garner2021].

Under the methodology approved by the SPM Interagency Technical Working
Group in September 2020, target year $T$ uses five years of CE Interview
collection quarters, $(T-5)$Q2 through $T$Q1 [@burnsfox2021;
@blsspmhome]. For consumer units with children, BLS constructs spending
on food, clothing, shelter, utilities, telephone, and internet (FCSUti),
including owners' mortgage-principal payments and imputed in-kind
benefits. The latter include broadband subsidies, energy assistance,
school lunches, WIC, and rental assistance. Spending is normalized to
the reference family using the three-parameter equivalence scale and
updated to target-year dollars with a composite FCSUti price index
[@betson1996; @garner2021].

Let $E$ denote the survey-weighted 47th–53rd percentile band of
reference-family FCSUti expenditures. If $SU$ denotes shelter and
utilities excluding telephone, the tenure-specific national threshold is

$$
B_{T,h}=s\left(1.2\,\overline{FCSUti}_{E}
-\overline{SU}_{E}+\overline{SU}_{E,h}\right).
$$

The pooled expenditure band defines the basic-needs amount. The 1.2
multiplier allows for other basic goods and services, and replacing the
pooled housing mean with the tenure-specific mean differentiates the
three thresholds. The anchor share $s$ is 0.82 in the revised official
series used here, compared with 0.83 in the preceding series
[@bls2026corrected].

The benchmark vintage is the corrected BLS 2005–2024 workbook issued in
July 2026, followed by the published 2025 values. In particular, historical
comparisons for 2019–2024 use the revised series rather than the values
available at each historical date. Source vintages matter when interpreting
a backtest [@croushore2001]; this paper does not reconstruct historical
information sets from the corrected series.

## Applying a threshold to an SPM unit

National estimation and unit-level application are distinct operations.
If $q(A,C)$ is the equivalence scale for an already classified unit with
$A$ adults and $C$ children, normalized to one for two adults and two
children, the unit receives the corresponding fraction of its tenure's
reference threshold. For integer counts $A\geq1$ and $C\geq0$, write
$q(A,C)=e(A,C)/3^{0.7}$, where

$$
e(A,C)=
\begin{cases}
1, & A=1,\ C=0,\\
1.41, & A=2,\ C=0,\\
(1+0.8+0.5(C-1))^{0.7}, & A=1,\ C\geq1,\\
(A+0.5C)^{0.7}, & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
$$

The two-adult, no-child case uses Census's stated constant 1.41
[@spmtechnical]. The counts describe SPM composition roles; assigning
those roles requires the resource-unit definition, not age counts alone.
For example, one adult with two children has
$q(1,2)=2.3^{0.7}/3^{0.7}$, while $q(2,2)=1$.
Geographic adjustment applies to the housing
portion. Writing that portion as share $a_{T,h}$ and the local relative
housing-cost index as $g$, the calculation is

$$
B_{T,h}^{\mathrm{unit}}
=B_{T,h}\,q(A,C)\left[(1-a_{T,h})+a_{T,h}g\right].
$$

The bracketed expression is the multiplier on the whole threshold; the
relative housing-cost index $g$ adjusts only the housing portion. Resources
below the resulting threshold imply SPM poverty; equality does not.
The resource definition and classification of adults, children, and SPM
units must be supplied consistently with the SPM framework. Estimating
national thresholds does not itself resolve those classifications.

::: {#tbl-current-release}
{{< include tables/current_release.md >}}

The shares sum the shelter and utilities components in the BLS shares
workbook and exclude telephone and internet.
:::

Both components in @tbl-current-release use published 2025 values
[@bls2025thresholds; @blsspmshares]. The geographic index is separately
dated and estimated. Published national inputs therefore do not make a
local threshold fully official when its geographic component is modeled.
Local estimation areas comprise metropolitan statistical areas and
Census's residual metropolitan and nonmetropolitan groups
[@spmtechnical]. Counties
identify the applicable area; county-specific thresholds are not
independently estimated. The annual geographic projection is described
in @sec-rolling.

# Replication from public consumption data {#sec-replication}

## Expenditure construction and estimation sample

The replication reads public CE Interview FMLI files for each target
year's five-year window. Previous-quarter and current-quarter expenditure
fields split a single three-month recall period; their sum is multiplied
by four to annualize spending. Utilities already include telephone, so
telephone is retained in FCSUti but removed when constructing the narrower
shelter-utilities measure. Mortgage principal is included using the FMLI
outlay fields [@cepumd; @blsspmhome].

The food redesign requires a further decision in pooled windows. Newer
records use a combined grocery summary in place of the earlier food
summaries. This implementation applies an 80-percent food allocation to
the combined summary; the BLS errata specifies a narrower item-code
allocation. This is a recorded approximation. Similarly, public FMLI
summaries do not directly provide the home-internet spending and in-kind
imputations required for a complete reproduction of the BLS procedure.
Those components are omitted here.

Each consumer unit's expenditures are normalized to the two-adult,
two-child reference family before estimating the weighted expenditure
band and tenure-specific housing means. The implementation uses CE
interview survey weights and an inclusive 47th–53rd percentile band from
a midpoint weighted cumulative distribution. It uses annual price
adjustments by collection year rather than BLS's quarterly treatment.
In the current replication, expenditure-deflation weights are derived
from the selected CE sample in each target year's window, before selecting
the percentile band; these differ from the fixed projection-comparator
weights described in @sec-projection.
Exact parity with BLS's percentile code has not been established.

Adult/child classification and housing tenure require explicit sample
rules. Independent minors can form CE consumer units, so minor-only
records do not establish the SPM adult/child classification needed for
exact equivalence scaling. The current research baseline excludes these
unresolved records. A sensitivity instead imposes one adult while retaining
the reported child count; that recode is nonofficial and does not resolve
membership. The baseline also excludes tenure codes 5 and 6 and assigns
code 3 to owners with a mortgage. These are research sample policies,
not a claim that BLS uses the same handling.

## Replicated levels and sample sensitivities

The current method reconstructs seven target years, 2019–2025.
@tbl-current-replication reports signed deviations from the revised
published thresholds. Differences vary by tenure and year, including
positive deviations for owners without mortgages in later windows.
The comparison measures the combined discrepancy; it does not identify
the contribution of any particular omitted component or sample rule.

::: {#tbl-current-replication}
{{< include tables/current_replication.md >}}

Signed current-method replication deviations from published national
thresholds. Negative values indicate a lower replication.
:::

::: {#tbl-current-sensitivity}
{{< include tables/current_sensitivity.md >}}

Unresolved-youth interviews and their weighted share of child-containing
CE interviews, with maximum absolute threshold changes across tenures
under separate youth-recode and tenure sensitivities. The latter includes
tenure codes 5 and 6 as renters. These overlapping windows reuse observations.
:::

The tenure sensitivity in @tbl-current-sensitivity reaches 1.74 percent.
The recorded windows contain no code-3 observations, so assigning that
code to owners without a mortgage has zero measured effect here; that
result supplies no evidence about samples in which the code is present.
The weighted shares describe consumer-unit interviews, not unique
population counts.

These are selected sensitivities, not an exhaustive error bound. Annual
rather than quarterly price adjustment, the food allocation, omitted
home internet and in-kind imputations, and percentile conventions remain
unmeasured sources of discrepancy. Sampling and imputation uncertainty
has not been estimated for the replication. Published BLS standard errors
provide scale for the level differences, but they do not account for
replication error or covariance from shared survey inputs.

# Projecting thresholds {#sec-projection}

## Price and consumption growth rules

The projection question is whether changes in public consumption data
improve on price adjustment of the latest published threshold. Let
$\widetilde B_{T,h}$ be the replicated national threshold and $P_T$ a
price index. Starting from an official base $B_{T-1,h}$, the combined rule
is

$$
\widehat B_{T,h}=B_{T-1,h}
\left[\lambda\frac{\widetilde B_{T,h}}{\widetilde B_{T-1,h}}
+(1-\lambda)\frac{P_T}{P_{T-1}}\right].
$$

We compare All-Items CPI-U adjustment; adjustment by a static-weight
composite matching the FCSUti components available in the data; the
replication growth ratio alone; and an equal blend of replication growth
and composite-price growth. The last three correspond to $\lambda=0$,
$1$, and $1/2$ when $P$ is the composite index. The blend weights are fixed
rather than fitted to the small evaluation sample.

The projection composite uses five CPI-U components: food, apparel,
shelter, fuels and utilities, and telephone services. Their respective
weights are $(0.30, 0.05, 0.45, 0.12, 0.04)/0.96$, with no separate
home-internet component. These are fixed research weights; they do not
reproduce the BLS deflator exactly. If $P_{i,T}$ is component $i$'s
annual-average index, the current projection's price multiplier is
$\sum_i w_i(P_{i,T}/P_{i,T-1})$. The frozen experiments use the same
normalized weights, with the fixed-2019-base backtest distinguished from
the prior-year-based 2025 nowcast below. These projection weights are
separate from the sample-derived weights used to adjust CE expenditures
in the current replication.

Using growth ratios has a specific rationale. If replication differs
from the official level by a stable proportional factor, that factor
cancels between adjacent years. A persistent additive difference need
not cancel, and changing omissions or sample effects can alter growth.
The method therefore requires empirical evaluation of the ratios, even
when the replicated levels appear stable.

CPI-U adjustment estimates a different process from annual re-estimation
of consumption thresholds. Census's analysis of the originally published
2024 SPM estimates illustrates the distinction: consumption-based
threshold growth exceeded the CPI-U update, and price-updating the
thresholds instead would have produced a 2024 rate of 12.4 percent, below
the published SPM rate [@creamer2025]. That finding concerns the published
vintage used in that analysis; it does not establish how a particular
projection rule will perform in every year.

## Current-method retrospective comparison {#sec-current}

@tbl-current-projection evaluates six one-year projections for 2020–2025.
For each target year, all rules start from the prior year's revised
published threshold. The current composite holds static component weights
and rebases the price index to each prior year. Replication and price
inputs use the versions recorded in the September 2026 research replay. Historical availability
of those exact versions is not inferred.

::: {#tbl-current-projection}
{{< include tables/current_projection.md >}}

Current-method retrospective mean absolute percentage errors across
three tenures, 2020–2025. The mean row weights the six years equally.
:::

Over these six years, the replication ratio has the lowest mean absolute
error, followed by the blend, composite-price adjustment, and CPI-U
adjustment. The table also shows substantial variation across years.
It uses realized prices, which would not have been available in a forecast
made before the target year's inflation was observed. Adjacent CE windows
share four of five years, and tenure estimates share observations. The
resulting errors are dependent retrospective evidence, not eighteen
independent forecast trials or six prospective validations.

## Frozen comparison used for the 2025 nowcast

The pre-committed 2025 estimate used an earlier, separately preserved
method version. Its 2020–2024 comparison is shown in @tbl-backtest. This
experiment also uses corrected actual thresholds and realized price
indices; it is retrospective. Its fixed-2019-base price composite and
sample treatment differ from the current research method. Keeping the
two tables separate preserves the evidence available when the 2025
nowcast was committed.

::: {#tbl-backtest tbl-colwidths="[34,11,11,11,11,11,11]"}
{{< include tables/backtest.md >}}

Frozen-method mean absolute percentage errors across three tenure
thresholds, projecting each year from the prior year's corrected values.
:::

CPI-U adjustment has a mean absolute error of 2.23 percent and understates
threshold growth in four of five years, with a signed mean error of
−1.9 percent. Composite-price adjustment reduces the mean absolute error
to 1.57 percent, removing about thirty percent of the CPI-U error in this
sample. The replication ratio scores 0.41 percent, with a signed mean of
+0.1 percent and annual signed means ranging from +0.5 to −0.3 percent.
The equal blend scores 0.76 percent; its annual signed means range from
−0.1 to −1.4 percent. These are descriptions of the frozen comparison,
not uncertainty intervals for future forecasts.

The blend remained the primary committed estimate although the final
frozen comparison ranked the replication ratio first. The method-version
and amendment chronology is recorded in Appendix A. The external
validation below reports every rule, including the original and amended
blend estimates, without choosing the primary forecast after seeing
published 2025 outcomes.

# Pre-committed 2025 validation {#sec-nowcast}

## The estimate before publication

At the commitment date, 2025 was a nowcasting problem: estimating a
quantity whose underlying period had occurred but whose official value
was unpublished [@giannone2008]. The relevant CE collection window,
2020Q2 through 2025Q1, and eleven months of 2025 CPI observations were
available. October 2025 CPI was not published; the recorded price inputs
use the eleven available months. BLS documents this annual-average
treatment for CPI series without a published October observation
[@blscpi2025shutdown].

The committed blend projected \$41,036.34 for owners with mortgages,
\$34,135.99 for owners without mortgages, and \$40,755.98 for renters.
It applies replication and composite-price growth to the corrected 2024
base fixed in the commitment.

::: {#tbl-nowcast tbl-colwidths="[31,17,18,14,20]"}
{{< include tables/nowcast.md >}}

Pre-committed 2025 nowcast for a two-adult, two-child unit, with its
replication and price components. These are model estimates.
:::

Replicated threshold growth ranged from 4.4 to 6.0 percent by tenure,
against 3.2 percent composite-price growth. Their blend projected
3.8 to 4.6 percent growth, compared with 2.6 percent realized CPI-U growth.
The nowcast price component chain-links at the prior year; the frozen
backtest composite holds a fixed 2019 base. Both definitions are recorded
with their experiments rather than treating them as interchangeable.

## Evaluation against published thresholds {#sec-evaluation}

BLS published the 2025 thresholds on August 24, 2026:
\$41,323 for owners with mortgages, \$34,326 for owners without, and
\$41,701 for renters [@bls2025thresholds]. The linked workbook carries
full-precision values and standard errors of \$327, \$560, and \$393.
BLS reports growth of 4.40 to 6.33 percent by tenure over the corrected
2024 base. All forecast evaluations below use that base as fixed before
publication.

::: {#tbl-evaluation tbl-colwidths="[34,17,17,16,16]"}
{{< include tables/evaluation.md >}}

Signed percentage errors against published 2025 thresholds and mean
absolute error across tenures. The CPI-U rule uses the pinned
eleven-month 2025 annual average; both committed blend vintages are shown.
:::

::: {#tbl-evaluation-levels tbl-colwidths="[24,16,18,12,15,15]"}
{{< include tables/evaluation_levels.md >}}

Published 2025 thresholds and the committed nowcast in dollars, with
BLS's stated growth and the projected growth.
:::

The amended blend understates the three thresholds by 0.69, 0.55, and
2.27 percent, giving a mean absolute error of 1.17 percent. Its signed
mean of −1.17 percent falls inside the −0.1 to −1.4 range described in
advance, although the renter error lies outside that range. The two
owner differences are within one published BLS standard error and the
renter difference is about 2.4 standard errors. These comparisons give
scale; the BLS standard errors are neither forecast uncertainty bands
nor a significance test of the model's discrepancies.

CPI-U adjustment understates all three thresholds by 1.70 to 3.47 percent,
for a mean absolute error of 2.58 percent. The replication ratio alone
scores 0.75 percent and has errors on both sides of zero; composite-price
adjustment scores 2.02 percent. The replication ratio therefore ranks
first in this validation year as well as in the frozen retrospective
comparison. The superseded original blend scores 0.98 percent, compared
with 1.17 percent for the amended blend. Both are reported because both
were committed before the official outcome. One year cannot establish
whether any of these rankings will persist.

The largest miss occurs for renters. BLS reports renter growth of 6.33
percent against 5.33 and 4.40 percent for the two owner tenures. The blend
projects renter growth of 3.92 percent, and replication alone 4.62
percent. This analysis does not identify the reason for the difference.
Omitted imputations, price treatment, sample classification, percentile
conventions, and other replication differences could affect growth;
the observed miss does not attribute it to any one of them.

## Validation of the price comparator

BLS publishes its FCSUti deflator growth alongside the thresholds,
providing an additional comparison after publication. This comparison uses
the fixed-2019-base composite from the frozen backtest, rather than the
prior-year-based composite used in the 2025 nowcast. The fixed-base
composite differs from the BLS index by at most 0.7 percentage point in
each year from 2020 through 2025, with a mean absolute gap of 0.4 point
and no consistent sign. This is evidence of closeness over those years,
not exact replication of the deflator.

For 2025, the BLS threshold page reports CPI-U growth of 2.70 percent,
compared with 2.63 percent implied by the eleven-month annual average in
the pinned CPI observations. The threshold page does not reconcile this
difference with the CPI program's documented eleven-month averaging
rule [@blscpi2025shutdown]. We retain the recorded calculation rather
than substituting a different annual average in the completed forecast
evaluation.

# Conditional forecasts beyond available microdata {#sec-rolling}

## Projecting expenditure records and rolling windows

The preceding comparisons observe the CE collection window for each
target year. A future projection instead supplies the unobserved quarters
and then re-estimates the threshold from the resulting twenty-quarter
window. The September 9, 2026 information snapshot uses observed CE
records through 2025Q1. At that cutoff, BLS scheduled the next annual CE
microdata release for October 29, 2026 [@blsce2025shutdown]. For each
later quarter the projection reuses the latest observed quarter of
the same season, preserving survey weights, composition, and record
identities. Monetary spending is multiplied by the cumulative price
change and an assumed real-expenditure growth factor. Historical quarters
leave the window as projected quarters enter; this is not a direct
inflation adjustment of the final threshold.

The prospective evaluation will also need to account for the interruption
of CE collection in October and November 2025. BLS describes adjustments
for its annual expenditure estimates and states that those adjustments
will not be applied directly to the public-use files
[@blsce2025shutdown]. This projection uses seasonal donor records; it
does not estimate the effect of that missing-data treatment on future
published SPM thresholds.

Let $r$ be an annual log growth rate for real expenditures. A donor
record from year $d$ projected to year $t$ receives the multiplier
$(P_t/P_d)\exp[r(t-d)]$. We report two scenarios: zero real growth and a
CE trend. To estimate the latter, we construct five nonoverlapping
annual collection blocks ending in 2021–2025, express them in common
origin-year prices with fixed origin-window component weights, and
compute each block's survey-weighted mean in the 47th–53rd percentile
FCSUti band. An ordinary least-squares regression of log means on year
provides a slope. The applied slope is half that estimate; the 0.5
shrinkage was declared independently of the reported forecast scores.

We report rates as compounded annual equivalents, $\exp(r)-1$, not as
the log rate $r$ that enters the multiplier. The applied annual
real-growth rate is 0.914 percent, from an applied log rate of 0.910
percent. Using ten annual blocks gives 0.817 percent; excluding the two
blocks ending in 2021 and 2022 from the five-block fit leaves three
blocks and gives −0.135 percent. These alternatives demonstrate
sensitivity to the fitting window. They are not confidence intervals:
repeated interviews, survey design, serial dependence, and future
structural changes are not captured by ordinary regression uncertainty.
The zero-real scenario supplies a separate comparison rather than a
lower statistical bound.

The nominal path uses annual CPI-U growth from CBO's February 2026
economic projections, rebased to the observed 2025 annual index
[@cbodata2026]. Applying that same growth rate to each expenditure price
component and to rents is an assumption of this projection, not a CBO
forecast for each component. Real growth and prices both affect projected
spending; setting real growth to zero still allows changes from replacing
older observations in the rolling window.

For origin $O=2025$, the national projection is

$$
\widehat B_{T,h}=B_{O,h}^{\mathrm{published}}
\frac{\widetilde B_{T,h}}{\widetilde B_{O,h}},\qquad
\widehat a_{T,h}=a_{O,h}^{\mathrm{published}}
\frac{\widetilde a_{T,h}}{\widetilde a_{O,h}}.
$$

Thus both the national base and housing share start from published
2025 values, with subsequent changes estimated from the projected
microdata. The percentile band is selected again for every target
window. Changes in band membership can make the tenure-specific
threshold under the positive-real-growth scenario slightly lower than
under zero real growth in a particular year; the scenarios do not
preserve a fixed ranking of selected observations.

::: {#tbl-rolling-projection}
{{< include tables/rolling_projection.md >}}

Conditional national reference thresholds under the CE-trend and
zero-real-growth scenarios. The 2025 bases are published; later values
are modeled. These scenarios do not constitute prediction intervals.
:::

## Projecting local relative housing costs

The geographic window for threshold year $T$ comprises ACS years
$T-5$ through $T-1$. Public-use geography requires fractional allocation
from Public Use Microdata Areas to SPM estimation areas. The projection
uses the declared February 2013 metropolitan delineation and records
the crosswalk and source vintages. These allocations, public-data
topcoding, and the public rental sample limit exact reproduction of
the Census calculation [@acs2024pumd].

The rental sample contains occupied, cash-rented two-bedroom housing
units with complete kitchen and plumbing facilities, positive gross
rent, and positive housing weights. This follows the housing-unit
definition used for the SPM geographic adjustment [@spmtechnical].
For each complete five-year PUMS product, we retain its housing weights
(`WGTP`) and identify survey-year cohorts from the record identifiers;
we do not combine overlapping products as independent observations.
Monthly gross rent is `GRNTP` multiplied once by `ADJHSG` divided by
$10^6$, placing the product's observations on a common dollar basis
[@acs2024accuracy]. Area estimation multiplies housing weights by the
PUMA-to-area allocation fractions. After sorting adjusted rents, the
median is the first observed value whose cumulative weight reaches
50 percent. This is a discrete weighted median without interpolation,
an additional approximation in the public-data reconstruction. Future
donor copies retain the original product weights; no annual reweighting
or population-growth adjustment is imposed.

Observed ACS cohorts are used through 2024. Each later cohort copies
the 2024 donor records, scales nominal rents, and converts them to a
common price basis. Local and national weighted rent medians are
recomputed from each complete five-cohort window. Equal nationwide
rent growth therefore does not imply constant local relative costs:
the mix changes as older observed cohorts leave the window. Once all
five cohorts use the same donor distribution, the relative indices
stabilize under this assumption. In this snapshot that occurs in 2029.
The whole-threshold factor can continue changing as the housing share
changes.

The public-data products used for the 2024 anchor and subsequent
windows differ. To avoid treating a product change as rent growth, we
bridge them over the common 2020–2023 years. If $m^{v}_{W,j}$ is area
$j$'s local-to-national rent-median ratio for window $W$ in product $v$,
then, for an area with a published 2024 anchor,

$$
\widehat g_{T,j}=g^{\mathrm{published}}_{2024,j}
\frac{m^{\mathrm{old}}_{2020:2023,j}}{m^{\mathrm{old}}_{2019:2023,j}}
\frac{m^{\mathrm{new}}_{T-5:T-1,j}}{m^{\mathrm{new}}_{2020:2023,j}}.
$$

Unpublished residual groups retain explicitly modeled, unanchored
indices. The menu contains 342 published and seven modeled areas in
2022, and 341 published and eight modeled areas from 2023. Annual
comparisons distinguish published-index revisions and assignment
changes from projected rent growth. In particular, the Massachusetts
nonmetropolitan published index changes between 2022 and 2023, and
Sumter County moves from a published residual group to an unanchored
modeled group; neither discontinuity is smoothed into a rent forecast.

# Discussion {#sec-discussion}

The results distinguish two tasks: estimating a threshold level and
projecting its growth. The public-data replication does not reproduce
every component of the official method, and its level discrepancies
remain material. Growth ratios can nevertheless be useful when some
proportional discrepancies persist across adjacent windows. Their
performance must be judged directly; agreement in levels is neither
necessary nor sufficient for accurate growth projections.

In the periods examined, consumption-based growth improves on CPI-U
adjustment as a predictor of published SPM thresholds. That pattern is
consistent with the measure's quasi-relative construction: annual
re-estimation can reflect consumption changes that price adjustment
alone omits. The results do not isolate how much of the difference is
attributable to real spending, relative prices, sample composition, or
in-kind benefits. They also do not make price-indexed anchored measures
inappropriate; those measures deliberately estimate a fixed real
standard rather than the threshold BLS will publish.

The evidence for prospective accuracy remains limited. The current
six-year comparison uses revised data and an implementation applied
after outcomes were known. The frozen five-year comparison informed a
single 2025 validation. Overlapping CE windows and shared tenure samples
reduce the independent variation in both comparisons. The replication
ratio's lower average errors therefore motivate further validation,
without establishing a universally preferred rule or fitted combination
weight.

The information horizon also matters. When the complete CE window is
available but BLS thresholds are not, consumption replication can supply
a nowcast. Beyond the available CE window, it requires assumptions about
future consumption as well as prices. The conditional extension here
specifies those assumptions and advances both survey windows, but its
longer-horizon accuracy has not been prospectively validated. Method
changes, benefit imputations, and changes in sample composition can
also alter growth relationships. The sample and trend sensitivities
identify specific uncertainties but do not provide forecast intervals.

Threshold choice affects modeled poverty through the distribution of
resources near the line, not through threshold growth alone. In a frozen
historical PolicyEngine simulation, projected SPM poverty under the
committed 2025 nowcast was 0.4 percentage points higher than under
CPI-U-adjusted thresholds. That simulation uses the model's CPI-U
parameters, rather than the realized annual-average CPI-U rule evaluated
above. The recorded sensitivity depends on its original population and
model vintage; it is not a result from the current model or a general
conversion between threshold errors and
poverty-rate errors. Its saved receipt lacks immutable model and dataset
identities, so an exact independent replay of this historical sensitivity
has not been established.

# Appendix A: method versions and forecast commitment {.unnumbered}

The frozen replication used for the 2025 commitment has mean absolute
deviations across tenures of 1.5 to 2.1 percent per year against revised
2019–2024 thresholds, and 1.0 to 1.6 percent against the preceding
published series with its corresponding anchor share. Published BLS
sampling standard errors span 0.7 to 2.1 percent of the revised threshold
levels in those years. These standard errors describe official threshold
estimation; they do not quantify the uncertainty of the replication.

::: {#tbl-replication}
{{< include tables/replication.md >}}

Frozen-method replication deviations by tenure, with the anchor share
matched to each reference vintage. These results are preserved separately
from the current-method replication.
:::

The original 2025 blend was committed before a correction to the
composite-price construction, which had combined CPI components without
putting them on a common index base. The correction changed the
retrospective method ranking; the equal blend was retained as the primary
forecast, and all component rules were included in the promised
external evaluation. This was one pre-publication amendment, not a rule
selected using the published 2025 outcome.

The amendment moved estimates by 0.1 to 0.3 percent: owners with
mortgages from \$41,099.57 to \$41,036.34, owners without from
\$34,250.70 to \$34,135.99, and renters from \$40,791.72 to \$40,755.98.
The original and amended values, corrected 2024 base, and evaluation
rules remain fixed in the repository. This use of preregistration
[@nosek2018] separates the recorded forecast from later method development.

The [August 7, 2026 archived page](https://web.archive.org/web/20260807211521/https://spm-threshold-paper.vercel.app/)
and retained OpenTimestamps evidence
precede the August 24 publication. The original forecast tags, manifests,
and proof files remain unchanged. A dated September 8 amendment corrects
two artifact hashes in a secondary manifest without claiming that its
old timestamp covers the amendment. The repository documents those
identities and checks the retained bytes; this revision does not
independently reverify blockchain attestations.

This paper makes no new forecast commitment or scheduled cutoff. The
previously discussed 2026 CE collection window already closed in 2026Q1.
Any future commitment would require an actual timestamp and a recorded
available-input cutoff before the outcome is published.

# Appendix B: reproducibility {.unnumbered}

The [paper repository](https://github.com/PolicyEngine/spm-threshold-paper)
provides the manuscript, table generators, verification tests, and
recorded inputs. Its [source-data provenance](https://github.com/PolicyEngine/spm-threshold-paper/blob/cc858aa610cc414215fe3e1fc4038b5248810743/data/PROVENANCE.md)
describes the preserved experimental collections. The
companion calculator source [@spmcalculator2026] contains the
expenditure and geographic estimators, source acquisition
scripts, and standalone implementation at the rolling projection's
exact revision.

The paper repository preserves the inputs and generated tables for the frozen
experiments, together with a separate current-method artifact containing
source hashes, methodology choices, and sample diagnostics. The
2019–2025 retrospective experiment retains its original implementation
pin, spm-calculator development version 0.5.0 at commit
`0d7fa0d77b0a88064ab7b9fe70557309b5f7901f`. The conditional rolling
projection uses the separate 1.0.0 release candidate at commit
`78bae15f76152c6076dd909a09f6b63dc2ec8c34`. The candidate's content
digest is:

```{.text .small}
3d86d5c4c0423480e6b69b75d222ffa4a7a2639e4094df5ba2504af01be17173
```

Exact source and release identities are recorded alongside the inputs;
`data/PROVENANCE.md` describes the separate collections. The frozen
poverty sensitivity additionally requires its original model and
population dataset to reproduce.

To verify the reported tables, clone the paper repository with its full
tag history and check out the manuscript revision being evaluated. Run
`python3 -B scripts/check_paper.py` and
`python3 -B -m unittest discover -s tests -v`. Quarto 1.9.36 and TeX Live
2026 render this revision with `quarto render --to html` and
`quarto render --to pdf`. These commands regenerate the tables from
the preserved artifacts; regenerating the underlying CE and ACS
estimates additionally requires the pinned calculator and its source
files. The repository README gives the build commands and separates
this verification from raw-data replication.

The rolling projection is a portable artifact shared by the paper and
standalone calculator, with year-specific national bases, housing shares,
geographic indices, assignments, and source fingerprints. The pinned
calculator includes PolicyEngine, Microcosm, and native Axiom adapters
that consume these quantities through explicit contracts. Population
sources supply native SPM membership and composition roles;
tax-benefit models retain responsibility for resources, including
ordinary income, program awards, and the housing-assistance cap, and the
population system retains its weights. A change of
rules engine does not require a second expenditure forecast. Runtime
parity and release integration are separate checks from the statistical
validity of the projection. The snapshot date does not reconstruct
historical information sets or certify a public deployment.

In population applications, the threshold's housing portion limits the
housing subsidy counted as an SPM resource. The accompanying resource
specification sums modeled awards within a household, allocates the total
to SPM units by member share, and applies each unit's cap after allocation,
following Census's subsidy proration [@spmtechnical, p. 14]. It treats
interview-time public or reduced-rent housing status as full-year
assistance to a program family represented by the householder's SPM unit,
because the survey does not identify that family. It allocates the tenant
contributions of units with positive awards by the same shares; Census
does not document this split, so it is a declared consistency assumption
rather than verified production parity. Program eligibility and awards
do not depend on the cap. These choices concern resource valuation and
do not change the threshold estimates reported here. They do not revise
the separately preserved historical poverty sensitivity.

Tables regenerate from the recorded artifacts. The build checks their
hashes before generating outputs in temporary storage and comparing the
results with the saved tables and evaluation JSON. Archived tables no
longer used in the manuscript remain preserved and checked. These checks
support reproducibility of the recorded experiments, while the method
limitations described above constrain their interpretation.
